questions.title: Symbiosis: both organisms benefit
questions.question: Symbiosis is?

options.A: One organism causes harm to other
options.B: One organism is benefited and the other is unaffected
options.C: Essential association of two organisms and both are benefited

explanations.A: Incorrect. One organism causing harm to the other describes parasitism, not symbiosis in the mutualistic sense tested here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. One organism benefiting while the other is unaffected describes commensalism, not symbiosis in this sense.
explanations.C: Correct. Symbiosis, in the strict mutualistic sense used in this bank, is an essential association between two organisms. Both partners benefit from the relationship. This is distinct from parasitism, where the host is harmed, and commensalism, where the host is unaffected.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since option C is the printed correct answer, "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Define symbiosis, in the mutualistic sense, as an association in which both organisms benefit.

questions.title: Facultative parasites are those either free-living or parasitic
questions.question: Facultative parasites are those?

options.A: Exist in a host in which it does not ordinary live
options.D: Remain all or most of its life in its host

explanations.A: Incorrect. Existing in a host it does not ordinarily live in describes an incidental (accidental) parasite, not a facultative one.
explanations.B: Correct. Facultative parasites are those that can be either free-living or parasitic. They switch between the two lifestyles depending on conditions. This is unlike an obligate parasite, which has no free-living option at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Being completely dependent upon its host describes an obligate parasite, the opposite of facultative flexibility.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Remaining all or most of its life in its host describes an obligate (or at least a highly host-dependent) parasite, not the free-living-capable facultative pattern.

questions.learning_objective: State that facultative parasites are those capable of being either free-living or parasitic.

questions.title: Obligatory parasite completely dependent on host
questions.question: Obligatory parasite are those?

options.C: A free-living that may live as parasitic

explanations.A: Incorrect. Being either free-living or parasitic describes a facultative parasite, not an obligate one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Occurring in one specific host is a host-specificity fact, not the same axis as obligate-vs-facultative dependency (many obligate parasites can still use more than one host species across their life cycle).
explanations.C: Incorrect. "A free-living [organism] that may live as parasitic" restates the facultative pattern, not the obligate one.
explanations.D: Correct. An obligatory parasite is completely dependent upon its host. It cannot survive outside a host at any stage of its life cycle. This total dependency is the defining feature that distinguishes it from a facultative parasite.

questions.learning_objective: State that obligatory parasites are those completely dependent upon their host.

questions.title: Opportunistic parasites cause disease in immunocompromised hosts
questions.question: Opportunistic parasite are those?

options.C: Exists in a host in which it does not ordinary live
options.D: A free-living but seeks its host from time to time

explanations.A: Correct. Opportunistic parasites are those that produce disease specifically in an immunocompromised host. Their pathogenicity is normally kept in check by an intact immune system. Once that check is lost, disease that would not otherwise occur can develop.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Producing disease in an immunocompetent host is the pattern of a true, primary pathogen, not an opportunistic one, which typically causes little or no disease when the immune system is intact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Existing in a host it does not ordinarily live in describes an incidental (accidental) parasite, a different category from opportunism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Being free-living but seeking a host occasionally describes a facultative parasite's behaviour, not the immune-status-dependent pattern that defines opportunism.

questions.learning_objective: State that opportunistic parasites are those that produce disease in an immunocompromised host.
